citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. Identify parenthesizations by the isometry fixing
elementary tensors: the product pairing is the same on their dense span,
so the map and its inverse extend to the completions. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $h\in H$, the map $C_h:H\to\mathbb C$, $C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$, is linear and bounded:
$|C_h(v)|=|(v,h)_1|\le\|h\|\,\|v\|$ by
[[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]].
For any Hilbert space $K$, identify $\mathbb C\widehat\otimes K$ with $K$
by $J_K(z\otimes v)=zv$. Every algebraic tensor is $1\otimes w$;
the tensor norm is then $\|w\|$, so $J_K$ extends to a surjective isometry
on the completion (with inverse $w\mapsto1\otimes w$).
Throughout the following formulas, $C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)}$ means
$J_{H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}}\circ(C_h\widehat\otimes I)$, with
$I$ the identity on $H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}$.
The bounded tensor-map supplier therefore applies and gives norm at most
$\|h\|$. This includes $n=1$, where $H^{\widehat\otimes0}=\mathbb C$.
Contraction commutes with permutations of the remaining $n-1$ factors,
so it takes symmetric or antisymmetric tensors to the corresponding
$(n-1)$-particle sector (and to $\mathbb C$ for $n=1$).

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h$ is the bounded functional above, its tensor extension is supplied by
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space, let $e\in H$ have norm one, and put
$K=e^\perp=\{v\in H:\langle e,v\rangle_2=0\}$. For
$\psi_m\in K_s^{(m)}$ and $k,m\ge0$, write
$|k\rangle:=e^{\otimes k}\in(\mathbb Ce)_s^{(k)}$ (with $|0\rangle=1$),
and define

$$J_{k,m}(|k\rangle\otimes\psi_m) =\sqrt{\binom{k+m}{k}}\, P_{s,k+m}(e^{\otimes k}\otimes\psi_m).$$

The map $J_{k,m}$ extends over the sector Hilbert tensor products and the
orthogonal direct sums to a unitary

$$J:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb Ce)\widehat\otimes\mathcal F_s(K) \longrightarrow\mathcal F_s(H).$$

Under this unitary, bosonic creation and annihilation by $e$ act on the first
factor as the one-mode ladder maps
$|k\rangle\mapsto\sqrt{k+1}|k+1\rangle$ and
$|k\rangle\mapsto\sqrt{k}|k-1\rangle$, respectively, tensored with the
identity on $\mathcal F_s(K)$, on finite-particle vectors.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ define the bosonic
creation and annihilation maps $a^\dagger(h)$ and $a(h)$ and the fermionic maps
$c^\dagger(h)$ and $c(h)$ as in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. Write $a_n(h)$ and $a_n^\dagger(h)$ for
their restrictions to the $n$th bosonic sector. For bosons set

$$D(a(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\},\qquad D(a^\dagger(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge0}\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}.$$

Then $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and $\mathcal F_a(H)$ are Hilbert spaces,
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense, and it is a graph core for both maximal
bosonic sector maps. The bosonic operators on their displayed domains are
closed and mutually adjoint, and on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ satisfy

$$[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad [a(h),a(k)]=[a^\dagger(h),a^\dagger(k)]=0.$$

The fermionic $c(h)$ and $c^\dagger(h)$ extend to bounded operators on the
whole Fock space, with norms $\|h\|$, and satisfy on the whole space

$$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad \{c(h),c(k)\}=\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0.$$

This is a mathematical construction of the two Fock representations; it does
not assign particle statistics to a physical species.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Throughout this page $H$ is a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with
inner product linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]).

A **(possibly unbounded) linear operator on $H$** is a linear map
$T:D(T)\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]) whose **domain** $D(T)\subseteq H$ is a linear
subspace ([[def-linear-subspace]]). The domain is part of the data: $T=S$ means
$D(T)=D(S)$ and $Tx=Sx$ for all $x\in D(T)$. One writes $T\subseteq S$, and
calls $S$ an **extension** of $T$, when $D(T)\subseteq D(S)$ and $Sx=Tx$ for
every $x\in D(T)$.

The **graph** of $T$ is
$$\Gamma(T):=\{(x,Tx):x\in D(T)\}\subseteq H\oplus H .$$
The direct sum $H\oplus H$ is read as the complex vector space of pairs with
coordinatewise operations and the inner product
$\langle (x,y),(u,v)\rangle=\langle x,u\rangle+\langle y,v\rangle$, whose induced
norm is
$$\|(x,y)\|=(\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2)^{1/2};$$
it is complete because $H$ is ([[def-complete-metric-space]]). The **graph norm**
on $D(T)$ is
$$\|x\|_T:=(\|x\|^2+\|Tx\|^2)^{1/2},$$
so that $x\mapsto(x,Tx)$ is an isometric isomorphism of $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$
onto $\Gamma(T)$ with the norm restricted from $H\oplus H$.

$T$ is **closed** when $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subset of $H\oplus H$. A linear
operator is determined by its graph, and the following elementary translations
are used silently below: $\Gamma(T)$ is a linear subspace of $H\oplus H$;
$\Gamma(T)\cap(\{0\}\oplus H)=\{(0,0)\}$; the image of $\Gamma(T)$ under the
first coordinate projection is $D(T)$; and $T\subseteq S$ if and only if
$\Gamma(T)\subseteq\Gamma(S)$. In particular a closed operator is exactly one
whose graph is a closed subspace of $H\oplus H$.

**Notation.** No boundedness of $T$ is assumed, and $T$ is frequently called
*unbounded* to stress this; a bounded everywhere defined operator on $H$ is the
special case $D(T)=H$ in which $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subspace by continuity.
The letter $I$ denotes the identity operator on $H$ with domain $H$.

**Completeness of $H\oplus H$.** If $(x_n,y_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in
$H\oplus H$, then $\|x_n-x_m\|\le\|(x_n-x_m,y_n-y_m)\|$ and
$\|y_n-y_m\|\le\|(x_n-x_m,y_n-y_m)\|$ show that $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ are Cauchy
in $H$; let $x,y$ be their limits. Then
$\|(x_n,y_n)-(x,y)\|^2=\|x_n-x\|^2+\|y_n-y\|^2\to0$, so $H\oplus H$ is
complete. Consequently a sequence in $H\oplus H$ converges exactly when its two
coordinate sequences converge in $H$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

derivations.claim: Under the unitary $J_u$ of [F2], the one-dimensional $n$th sector of $\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C u)$ is spanned by the unit vector $e_n$. Therefore $Q_n$ are mutually orthogonal projections and their strong sum is the identity on $\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C u)$. Tensoring with the identity on $\mathcal F_s(K)$ and conjugating by $J_u$ shows that each $P_n$ is an orthogonal projection, $P_nP_m=0$ for $n\ne m$, and $\sum_{n\ge0}P_n\Psi=\Psi$ in norm for every $\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H)$.

For Borel $B$, the orthogonal sum defining $E_u(B)$ converges strongly because $\sum_n\|P_n\Psi\|^2=\|\Psi\|^2$. It is an orthogonal projection, $E_u(\varnothing)=0$, $E_u(\mathbb R)=I$, and orthogonality gives $E_u(B)E_u(C)=E_u(B\cap C)$. For pairwise disjoint Borel sets $B_j$, their intersections with $\mathbb N_0$ partition $B\cap\mathbb N_0$, so the corresponding orthogonal series gives $E_u(\bigcup_jB_j)\Psi=\sum_jE_u(B_j)\Psi$ in norm. Thus $E_u$ is a PVM supported on $\mathbb N_0$, and $E_u(\{n\})=P_n$.

Under $J_u$, $N_u$ is the diagonal operator $(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}\mapsto(n\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}$ with domain $\sum_n n^2\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty$. It is symmetric because every diagonal coefficient $n$ is real. If $\Phi$ lies in its adjoint domain with adjoint value $\Xi$, testing the adjoint identity on vectors supported in a single sector forces $\Xi_n=n\Phi_n$ for every $n$. Since $\Xi$ is square-summable, $\sum_n n^2\|\Phi_n\|^2<\infty$, so $\Phi\in D(N_u)$. Conversely, for $\Phi\in D(N_u)$, Cauchy–Schwarz on the sector sum gives the adjoint identity with value $N_u\Phi$. Hence $D(N_u^*)=D(N_u)$ and $N_u^*=N_u$, and its projections are the constructed $E_u(\{n\})=P_n$.

By [F2], on a one-mode occupation vector $e_n\otimes\phi$ one has $a(u)(e_n\otimes\phi)=\sqrt n\,e_{n-1}\otimes\phi$ and $a^\dagger(u)(e_n\otimes\phi)=\sqrt{n+1}\,e_{n+1}\otimes\phi$; thus $a^\dagger(u)a(u)=N_u$ on finite-particle vectors, including the $n=0$ sector. On the same invariant subspace, [F3] gives $a(u)a^\dagger(u)=a^\dagger(u)a(u)+I$. Consequently
$$N_u(N_u-I)=a^\dagger(u)a(u)a^\dagger(u)a(u)-a^\dagger(u)a(u)=a^\dagger(u)^2a(u)^2$$
on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, by substitution of the CCR and cancellation of the two $a^\dagger(u)a(u)$ terms.

Let $\Psi$ lie in the domain of $N_u(N_u-I)$ and truncate its one-mode occupation to $\Psi^{(M)}=\sum_{n=0}^{M}P_n\Psi$. The tail of the squared graph norm is $\sum_{n>M}(1+n^2(n-1)^2)\|P_n\Psi\|^2$, which tends to zero by the domain condition. For fixed $M$, write each $P_n\Psi$ under $J_u^{-1}$ as $e_n\otimes\phi_n$ with $\phi_n\in\mathcal F_s(K)$. Finite-particle vectors are dense in $\mathcal F_s(K)$ by [F1]; approximate each of the finitely many $\phi_n$ by such a vector. The one-mode unitary preserves norm, and on $n\le M$ the multiplier $n(n-1)$ is bounded, so these approximations also converge in graph norm. Their images under $J_u$ have finite total particle number. Thus $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a graph core for $N_u(N_u-I)$, and the finite-core normal-ordered identity of step 3.1 determines this closed extension.

risk_review.notes: Authoring consistency review checked every numbered argument against its named facts, exact supplier interface, stated domains and boundary assumptions. This record is not independent proof approval.

formulation.evidence: The Postulate explicitly defines the normalized transverse wavepacket, the mode count PVM, trace probabilities, factorial moments and dimensionless g² statistic.

scope.evidence: The postulate limits itself to one ideal normalized wavepacket mode, unit efficiency and no mismatch/background/dark counts; it excludes time response, point-field products and empirical outcomes.

sources.evidence: The item cites and the coverage record documents full-text reading of Glauber §II–IV and Steck Chapters 2 and 16 at exact locators; both support context while preserving the local mode assumptions.

non_derivation.evidence: The Postulate states the detector law is an additional adopted physical assumption, not deduced from CCR or free-field equations; the existing finite-instrument supplier is not claimed to imply a countable-outcome instrument.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice and use the positive transverse free-photon model whose one-particle space is $\mathcal H_T=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3)$ with its transverse condition and whose state space is the bosonic Fock space $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$. In the unit convention where $\mathbf k$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$, let $u\in\mathcal H_T^\nu$ be a normalized transverse wavepacket for the invariant measure $d\nu=d^3\mathbf k/(2|\mathbf k|)$, so that $u(\mathbf k)$ has unit metre and $\int|u|^2d\nu=1$. Let $v=Wu$, where $Wf(\mathbf k)=f(\mathbf k)/\sqrt{2|\mathbf k|}$; then $v\in\mathcal H_T$, $v(\mathbf k)$ has unit $\mathrm m^{3/2}$, and $\|v\|_2=1$. In the Fock factorization $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)\cong\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C v)\widehat\otimes\mathcal F_s(v^\perp)$, $P_n(v)$ is the orthogonal projection onto mode occupation $n$ tensored with the identity on the orthogonal-mode Fock factor. These projections are mutually orthogonal and have strong sum $I$; their count PVM is $E_v(B)=\sum_{n\in B\cap\mathbb N_0}P_n(v)$, and $N_v=\sum_n nP_n(v)$ on the domain $\sum_n n^2\|P_n(v)\Psi\|^2<\infty$. A density operator $\rho$ means a positive self-adjoint trace-class operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$, using the trace pairing obtained from the Fock space's second-variable-linear convention by conjugation. For $n\in\mathbb N_0$, put $p_n=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_n(v))$. The mathematical density/PVM result makes $(p_n)$ a countably additive probability law under the stated Countable Choice hypothesis.

Adopt as the ideal detector postulate that this law is the model probability for recording exactly $n$ photons in the selected mode. The detector is number resolving, has unit mode efficiency, and has no mode mismatch, background counts or dark counts. This is an additional physical measurement assumption; it is not deduced from the CCR or from the free-field equations.

When $\sum_n np_n<\infty$ and $\sum_n n(n-1)p_n<\infty$, define the first number moment and normally ordered second factorial moment by
$$\mu_v(\rho):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}np_n,\qquad F^{(2)}_v(\rho):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n(n-1)p_n.$$
The PVM sums define the unbounded-state moments. In this ideal mode model, define the normally ordered second-mode correlation to be the spectral factorial expectation $F^{(2)}_v(\rho)$. The self-adjoint closure of the finite-particle operator $a^\dagger(v)^2a(v)^2$ is $N_v(N_v-I)$ by [[lem-qftx-mode-number-pvm]], so this definition agrees with the normally ordered operator on its finite-particle core and uses the spectral expectation for states outside that core. It does not assert a trace product of $\rho$ with an unbounded operator. If $\mu_v(\rho)>0$, define the dimensionless same-mode zero-delay statistic
$$g_v^{(2)}(0):=\frac{F^{(2)}_v(\rho)}{\mu_v(\rho)^2}.$$
Here $0$ is the conventional zero-delay label for this same-mode statistic; no temporal detector response or pointwise product of electric-field distributions is defined.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear pairing used for bosonic Fock space, and let $u\in H$ satisfy $\|u\|=1$. Put $K=u^\perp$. Let $J_u:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C u)\widehat\otimes\mathcal F_s(K)\to\mathcal F_s(H)$ be the one-mode Fock unitary, and for $n\in\mathbb N_0$ let $e_n=u^{\otimes n}\in(\mathbb C u)_s^{(n)}$, with $e_0=1$. On $\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C u)$ define $Q_n z=\langle e_n,z\rangle_2e_n$, and on $\mathcal F_s(H)$ put
$$P_n:=J_u(Q_n\otimes I)J_u^{-1}.$$
For every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$, define the strong sum
$$E_u(B):=\sum_{n\in B\cap\mathbb N_0}P_n.$$
Define the mode number operator
$$N_u:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}nP_n,\qquad D(N_u):=\left\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n^2\|P_n\Psi\|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
Then $(P_n)_{n\ge0}$ are mutually orthogonal projections with strong sum $I$, $E_u$ is a projection-valued measure supported on $\mathbb N_0$, and $N_u$ is self-adjoint with these spectral projections. The diagonal operator $N_u(N_u-I)$ has domain $\{\Psi:\sum_n n^2(n-1)^2\|P_n\Psi\|^2<\infty\}$, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a graph core for it. On the finite-particle subspace,
$$N_u=a^\dagger(u)a(u),\qquad N_u(N_u-I)=a^\dagger(u)^2a(u)^2.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem (The recursion theorem) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$, there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$. Induction (The principle of mathematical induction): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ (The von Neumann naturals form a Peano system) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
(Zero and one under multiplication) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
(Cancellation for multiplication by a nonzero factor). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ (Addition is cancellative). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
(Multiplication is associative, Multiplication is commutative) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional (Multiplication of natural numbers), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Here $|A|^{1/2}$ denotes the unbounded PVM integral $f(E_A)$ for $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{1/2}$, with domain $D(f(E_A))=\{\psi:\int |\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty\}$ as in [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

derivations.claim:
The coefficients of $\psi_\alpha$ are square-summable because their squared norms sum to $Z_\lambda^{-1}\sum_n\lambda^n/n!=1$ by [F2]; the orthogonal one-mode sectors therefore make $\psi_\alpha$ a unit vector and [F6] makes its rank-one state a density operator. Its count probabilities are $p_n=Z_\lambda^{-1}\lambda^n/n!$ by [A1] and [F1]. Shifting indices in the nonnegative exponential series gives
$$\mu=Z_\lambda^{-1}\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{n\lambda^n}{n!}=\lambda,\qquad F_2=Z_\lambda^{-1}\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{n(n-1)\lambda^n}{n!}=\lambda^2,$$
so $g_v^{(2)}(0)=1$. The same calculation shows both required moments are finite.
For $\psi_m$, [F1] gives $p_n=\mathbf1_{n=m}$, hence $\mu=m$ and $F_2=m(m-1)$. Since $m\ge1$, the denominator is positive, and substitution into [A1] gives $g_v^{(2)}(0)=m(m-1)/m^2=1-1/m$.

The weights $(1-r)r^n$ are nonnegative and sum to one by [F4], so [F6] makes $\rho_r$ a density operator and [A1] gives the geometric count law $p_n=(1-r)r^n$. By Tonelli [F5],
$$\left(\sum_{j\ge0}r^j\right)^2=\sum_{i,j\ge0}r^{i+j}=\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)r^n.$$
Therefore $\sum_{n\ge0}nr^n=(1-r)^{-2}-(1-r)^{-1}=r/(1-r)^2$. Applying Tonelli to the triple product and counting the $(i,j,k)\in\mathbb N_0^3$ with $i+j+k=n-2$ gives
$$r^2\left(\sum_{j\ge0}r^j\right)^3=\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{n(n-1)}2r^n,$$
because that finite set has $\sum_{i=0}^{n-2}(n-1-i)=n(n-1)/2$ elements. Hence $\sum_{n\ge0}n(n-1)r^n=2r^2/(1-r)^3$. Multiplying by $1-r$ gives $\mu=r/(1-r)>0$ and $F_2=2r^2/(1-r)^2<\infty$, so [A1] yields $g_v^{(2)}(0)=2$.

Assume the ideal wavepacket counting postulate for a normalized mode $v$, and let $p_n$ be the resulting count law of a prepared state. Write
$$\mu:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}np_n,\qquad F_2:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n(n-1)p_n,\qquad g_v^{(2)}(0):=F_2/\mu^2$$
when $0<\mu<\infty$ and $F_2<\infty$. Let $J_v:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C v)\widehat\otimes\mathcal F_s(v^\perp)\to\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$ be the one-mode Fock unitary, let $|n\rangle_v=v^{\otimes n}$ with $|0\rangle_v=1$, and let $\Omega_{v^\perp}$ be the vacuum in $\mathcal F_s(v^\perp)$. Put $\psi_n:=J_v(|n\rangle_v\otimes\Omega_{v^\perp})$. For a unit vector $\psi$, $g_v^{(2)}(0;\psi)$ denotes the postulate's value for the pure density operator $|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ put $\lambda=|\alpha|^2$, $Z_\lambda=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\lambda^n/n!$, and define the coherent-mode vector
$$\psi_\alpha:=Z_\lambda^{-1/2}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\alpha^n}{\sqrt{n!}}\psi_n.$$
For $m\ge1$, the number preparation is $\psi_m$. For $0<r<1$, the geometric one-mode state is
$$\rho_r:=(1-r)\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}r^n|\psi_n\rangle\langle\psi_n|.$$
Then the ideal model predictions are
$$g_v^{(2)}(0;\psi_\alpha)=1,\qquad g_v^{(2)}(0;\psi_m)=1-\frac1m,\qquad g_v^{(2)}(0;\rho_r)=2.$$
The final state has the specified single-mode geometric occupation law; these conclusions do not classify all radiation as coherent, number, or thermal.

derivations.claim: Fix $n\in\mathbb N_0$ and average on its finite fiber using $Q_n$. For each $j\le n$, factorization gives $\sum_xQ_n(\{x\})X_{n,j}(x)=\eta$, and for distinct $i,j\le n$ it gives $\sum_xQ_n(\{x\})X_{n,i}(x)X_{n,j}(x)=\eta^2$. Since $K(n,x)=\sum_{j=1}^nX_{n,j}(x)$ and $K(n,x)(K(n,x)-1)=\sum_{i\ne j}X_{n,i}(x)X_{n,j}(x)$ for zero-one coordinates, it follows that $\sum_xQ_n(\{x\})K(n,x)=n\eta$ and $\sum_xQ_n(\{x\})K(n,x)(K(n,x)-1)=n(n-1)\eta^2$. For $n=0$ or $n=1$ the relevant sums are empty and the same formulas hold.

Using the Statement's encoding, identify $\Omega$ with a subset of $\mathbb N_0\times\mathbb N_0$. For either $Y=K$ or $Y=K(K-1)$, extend $f_Y(n,m):=p_nQ_n(\{x\})Y(n,x)$ by zero outside that subset. Counting measure on $\mathbb N_0$ is sigma-finite, so [F2] applied to the product of the two counting-measure spaces permits the nonnegative sum to be regrouped over the finite fibers. Using step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E K=\sum_np_n n\eta=\eta\mu$ and $\mathbb E[K(K-1)]=\sum_np_n n(n-1)\eta^2=\eta^2F_2$. Both are finite by hypothesis. Since $\eta\mu>0$, division gives $g_K^{(2)}(0)=\eta^2F_2/(\eta\mu)^2=F_2/\mu^2=g_N^{(2)}(0)=g_v^{(2)}(0)$ by [F1].

Assume the ideal wavepacket-counting postulate for a selected mode $v\in\mathcal H_T$ with $\|v\|=1$, and let $\rho$ be the incoming density operator on $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$ (a positive self-adjoint trace-class operator with trace one). By that postulate, $P_n(v)$ are the mode-count projections and $p_n=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_n(v))$ are the count probabilities, so $p_n\ge0$ and $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}p_n=1$. Define the incoming mean and second factorial moment by
$$\mu:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}np_n,\qquad F_2:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n(n-1)p_n,$$
and assume $0<\mu<\infty$ and $F_2<\infty$. Define $g_N^{(2)}(0):=F_2/\mu^2$; for this input state $\rho$, the postulate denotes the same statistic by $g_v^{(2)}(0)$.

Let $0<\eta\le1$ be a dimensionless fixed efficiency and assume no background or dark counts. To specify independent recording, put $b_\eta(0)=1-\eta$, $b_\eta(1)=\eta$, and
$$\Omega:=\{(n,x):n\in\mathbb N_0,\ x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\},\qquad \mathcal A:=\mathcal P(\Omega).$$
This is countable under the explicit encoding $(n,x)\mapsto(n,\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j2^{j-1})$. Give the space the point masses
$$\mathbb P(\{(n,x)\}):=p_n\prod_{j=1}^{n}b_\eta(x_j),$$
where the empty product for $n=0$ is $1$. For each fixed $n$, the product factors define the conditional product law $Q_n$ on $\{0,1\}^n$; hence its coordinates are independent Bernoulli variables with success probability $\eta$. Since $\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}Q_n(\{x\})=(\eta+(1-\eta))^n=1$, these point masses sum to one and define a probability measure $\mathbb P$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal A)$. Define $N(n,x):=n$ and $K(n,x):=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j$. For every nonnegative random variable $Y$ on this space, use the expectation
$$\mathbb E Y:=\sum_{(n,x)\in\Omega}Y(n,x)\,\mathbb P(\{(n,x)\}).$$
The marginal law of $N$ is $(p_n)$, and the conditional count law of $K$ given $N=n$ is the binomial law induced by $Q_n$. If $\mathbb E K>0$, define $g_K^{(2)}(0):=\mathbb E[K(K-1)]/(\mathbb E K)^2$. Then
$$\mathbb E K=\eta\mu,\qquad \mathbb E[K(K-1)]=\eta^2F_2.$$
Consequently the normalized zero-delay factorial correlation is unchanged:
$$g_K^{(2)}(0)=\frac{\mathbb E[K(K-1)]}{(\mathbb E K)^2}=\frac{F_2}{\mu^2}=g_N^{(2)}(0)=g_v^{(2)}(0).$$
This is a model deduction conditional on independent constant-efficiency thinning; it is not a universal property of real detectors.
